    Computation Inside Language Models

    5 minute read

    A language model asked to multiply two matrices can write a program and hand it to an external runtime. Now imagine that its next forward pass executes an instruction from that program. The following pass executes another. Eventually, the answer is sitting in memory maintained by the model. The visible chat might look the same, but the division of labor has changed.

    Four projects explore that boundary. Percepta builds a WebAssembly executor and later a Python environment with writable memory. qwenGPU adds a small parallel machine to Qwen. qwenLab gives Qwen an internal training lab for smaller transformers. Together, they separate three decisions that are easy to conflate: who chooses the computation, where it runs, and where its state persists.

    A transformer that executes WebAssembly

    In Can LLMs Be Computers?, Percepta compiles C programs to WebAssembly and runs them through an interpreter implemented in transformer weights. The model generates an execution trace whose tokens record operations such as changes to memory and the instruction pointer. Each step retrieves relevant information from previous steps. The authors demonstrate this with programs including a Sudoku solver and a minimum-cost matching algorithm. Percepta, Can LLMs Be Computers?

    A growing trace creates a performance problem. Standard full attention examines an increasingly long prefix at each decoding step. Percepta’s executor uses two-dimensional hard-max attention heads, where selecting the best key can be treated as a geometric query over a convex hull. In that structured setting, the authors describe logarithmic lookup time in the trace length in place of a linear scan. The speed claim concerns those lookups under the executor’s constraints. Percepta, Exponentially Fast Attention

    qwenGPU puts a small parallel machine inside Qwen

    qwenGPU inserts 45 constructed layers ahead of Qwen3.5-2B’s original layers. These implement a four-lane machine in which lanes run instructions together and can take different branches. Registers and memory live in the recurrent state of Gated DeltaNet layers. Generated execution records show which blocks run and which values they produce. qwenGPU repository

    The host compiles CUDA source to PTX, lowers it to the machine’s supported instructions, loads the program and inputs, and retrieves the output. The added model layers carry out the instructions. The repository reports that its reference interpreter matched a Tesla T4 on 49 test kernels and that checked model launches matched the interpreter. In a separate chat test, Qwen wrote a correct kernel on its first attempt for four of five sampled questions. That distinction matters because exact execution preserves the behavior of whatever program the model supplied, including a mistaken one. qwenGPU results

    qwenLab trains smaller transformers inside the model

    qwenLab appends 2,382 constructed layers to Qwen3.5-9B. The lab holds six experiments, each with a small transformer learning addition modulo 97. Its layers maintain learner weights and optimizer state, run forward and backward passes, apply AdamW updates, and evaluate the learners. The base Qwen model chooses commands and settings under a supplied protocol. The system therefore has two levels of learning behavior: the small transformers update their parameters while Qwen selects experiments with its own weights fixed. qwenLab repository

    In the reported session, the best selected fork achieved 49.09% test accuracy versus 15.68% for the control. That result comes from one run with a fixed protocol and a narrow search over learning rate and weight decay. The authors report about 0.64 seconds per internal training update versus 5.5 milliseconds for the same update in PyTorch on the same H100. The demonstration shows how much of a training workflow can run inside a model, including branching an experiment and comparing its results. qwenLab results and limits

    Spotlight gives a fixed executor an extensible memory

    Percepta’s second article asks what an executor can gain by keeping code and data in writable memory. Its Spotlight architecture addresses a small number of memory cells per token, so the amount of memory accessed at each step can stay fixed as the stored state grows. The authors use a hand-built Python environment to demonstrate package loading and replacement. The same execution module can run a different procedure after its memory changes. Percepta, Can LLMs Grow Their Own Capabilities?

    One demonstration stores the weights of a digit classifier in memory. The execution module reads the weights in chunks and evaluates the classifier. This is a concrete example of capability growth through loading a procedure or model into memory. The article’s longer-term proposal is that a system could also discover, validate, and retain its own methods over time. The package and classifier examples demonstrate the mechanism for using added capabilities. Percepta, Can LLMs Grow Their Own Capabilities?

    Where a reusable capability lives

    These projects connect to a question from my earlier post on computational words. Suppose a model identifies a repeated procedure and gives it a name. The name makes it easier to refer to the procedure. A separate design decision determines what happens when the name is used. Creating New Words

    A compiler can build the procedure’s execution rules into layers. An interpreter can run code supplied as tokens. A memory architecture can keep that code available across invocations and replace it when a better version arrives. From this perspective, qwenLab illustrates how a model can choose among actions offered by a built-in subsystem, while Spotlight illustrates how the set of available procedures can change after the executor is built.

    The distinction matters when evaluating a claim that a model gained a capability. Running a supplied program tests execution. Keeping that program available tests storage and retrieval. Discovering a program worth retaining, verifying it, and applying it to a new problem would test something further. Each step can be evaluated on its own, which gives a more precise account of what improved and where that improvement resides.
